name: The Junipers of Kochozenji

location.address: 505 Ayusawa, Minami-Alps City, Yamanashi Prefecture (古長禅寺, 山梨県南アルプス市鮎沢505)

access: Free, temple grounds open daily 9:00-17:00 year-round (境内自由・無休). Public Zen temple courtyard, no appointment needed.
transport: About 40 minutes by bus from Kofu Station
story:
There are four of them, one at each corner of the courtyard, and the tradition holds that they stand for the Four Heavenly Kings.

Kochozenji is a Rinzai Zen temple founded in 1316 by Muso Kokushi, and the planting of these Chinese junipers is attributed to him at that founding. That is where the figure of about 700 years comes from: a date on the temple, carried across to the trees, rather than anything measured in the wood. Locals call them the Yotsu-byakushin, the four byakushin. They sit roughly ten metres apart around the front court of what used to be the guest hall, and the state lists them as one thing, a single National Natural Monument since 14 November 1953.

They are not matching specimens. Girth at 1.5 metres runs from 2.00 to 3.90 metres across the four, and height from 11.20 to 17.70 metres, so the corners of the courtyard are visibly unequal.

The temple was the family temple of Oi-fujin, mother of Takeda Shingen, the warlord whose cavalry decided the shape of this province in the sixteenth century. If the founding tradition holds, the junipers were already two centuries into their growth when she came here to pray.

The courtyard is open nine to five, every day of the year. There is nothing to pay and nobody to ask.

name: The Great Zelkova of Mitsue

location.address: 1509 Terabe, Minami-Alps City, Yamanashi Prefecture (山梨県南アルプス市寺部1509), on the site of a former shrine, now municipal (city-owned) land

access: Free, no ticket. Stands on municipal land (the site of a former, now-vanished shrine), reached by public residential streets/alleys; OSM shows no private-access restriction on the approach roads. Honest caveat: the lane in is narrow with no dedicated parking, and it sits among houses, so visitors should be quiet and considerate of residents.
transport: About 30 minutes by bus from JR Kofu Station to Nakajo-iriguchi stop, then about 15 minutes on foot; about 10 minutes by car from the Chubu-Odan Expressway's Minami-Alps IC
story:
It looks like two trees leaning together. It is one, and the space between them is where lightning burned out its heart.

The Great Zelkova of Mitsue is counted among the Three Great Zelkovas of Japan, with Haramachi's in Gunma and Higashine's in Yamagata. A lightning fire hollowed and destroyed the central core long ago, leaving a trunk that reads as a pair from any distance; the base settles it as one tree. Around that trunk at chest height the national heritage database and the city's own page both give about 14.2 to 14.35 metres. An older source says 14.7. At the roots it swells to roughly 17.28 metres. Height is 20 metres in some accounts and 25 in the city's, and nobody has reconciled the two.

It was designated a National Natural Monument on 30 November 1928, one of the earliest listings in the country, on size alone. Its age is given as over a thousand years, and neither official source narrows that, so neither will we.

In October 2019 Typhoon Hagibis snapped a major limb off the north side. The city dressed and disinfected the wound and braced what was left on cables, finishing the work in February 2020, by which point the tree was already throwing new shoots from the base.

A shrine stood here once. It has gone; the tree outlasted it. The lane in is narrow and residential, so come quietly.
